catalog_quote: In Ngan’gityemerri, we need to operate with three stress rules; a syllable-timed stress rule for monomorphemic nominals; a second morpheme-timed stress rule for multi-morphemic nominals; and a third for the verbal complex in which stress serves to signal the auxiliary - complex verb stem constituency. [...] Stress placement on monomorphemic nominals and free form grammatical particles and postpositions is relatively straightforward. They bear primary stress on their initial syllable, and secondary stress on every second subsequent syllable unless that syllable is word-final. The final syllables of a mono-morphemic nominal can never bear stress. [...] Summarising stress patterns in Ngan'gityemerri: -We have seen that simple (monomorphemic) nouns, and 'simple verbs' (those consisting minimally of 'subject-auxiliary root' sequences) have a syllable-timed stress pattern with primary stress on the first syllable and secondary stress on the third syllable if it is not word-final.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the first syllable of the phonological word in every word type: monomorphemic nominals and particles (initial syllable), compounds and reduplications (initial syllable of the first morpheme), class-prefixed nouns (the prefix, being word-initial, takes primary stress; proclitic class markers are outside the word), simple verbs (initial syllable = bound subject pronoun) and complex verbs (initial syllable of the auxiliary). Secondary stress is where the rules differ: alternating (every second following syllable, never final) in simple nominals; morpheme-initial in compounds/reduplications; on the initial syllable of the complex verb stem in complex verbs, regardless of syllable count.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Monomorphemic nominals: on every second syllable after the first, never word-final (p. 90). Reduplications: full stress marking copied onto both elements; compounds: secondary on the initial syllable of the second morpheme irrespective of distance, so contiguous stresses occur (pp. 91-92). Simple verbs: secondary on the 3rd syllable if penultimate, but object-pronoun suffixes attract it to their own initial syllable (pp. 96-97). Complex verbs: secondary on the initial syllable of the complex verb stem; a serialised auxiliary adds a further secondary stress; tense/aspect enclitics never stressed, but without enclitics stress can fall on the final syllable of a complex verb (pp. 97-99). Perceptual correlates: higher pitch and greater amplitude (p. 90).
new_statements.exceptions: wamumu 'policeman' has stress on the class marker (lexically reanalysed base, fn. 23 p. 93); trimorphemic compounds show variation between morpheme-timed and syllable-timed patterns (p. 92); Reid states (p. 3) that the NgW and NgK dialects differ in stress rules. Hoddinott & Kofod 1988: 27-28, describing the Ngankikurungkurr (NgK) dialect, give primary stress on the first OR second syllable (trisyllables both ways, e.g. 'de.ngi.ni vs de.'tye.ngi; five-syllable class-prefixed words on the second syllable, a.'tye.rri.'wu.sye) with secondary stress usually penultimate and the final syllable never stressed — i.e. the two grammars disagree on whether a class prefix or the root-initial syllable carries primary stress (Reid, whose data are mainly NgW, gives initial stress on detyengi (K) and a-tyeri-wusye).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (Reid's unit; class proclitics excluded, prefixes and the auxiliary+verb-stem complex included); elicited/citation forms from fieldwork; H&K likewise word-level, explicitly 'not phonologically contrastive'.
new_statements.identity_note: Reid 1990 uses 'Ngan'gityemerri' as the language name covering two dialects, Ngan'giwumirri (NgW, Peppimenarti; the bulk of Reid's data, p. 24) and Ngan'gikurunggurr (NgK, Nauiyu/Daly River); Glottolog nang1259 'Nangikurrunggurr' (ISO nam) is the language-level node with no child dialects listed, so both fall under this key. Hoddinott & Kofod 1988 describe the NgK dialect specifically (as Ngankikurungkurr); Reid notes the dialects' stress rules differ, and the two grammars do differ on class-prefixed and some trisyllabic words.

sources.citation: Hoddinott, W. G. & F. M. Kofod. 1988. The Ngankikurungkurr language (Daly River area, Northern Territory). Pacific Linguistics D-77. Canberra: Dept of Linguistics, RSPacS, ANU. viii+346 pp.
sources.quote: Although stress is clearly perceptible it is not phonologically contrastive and is in the main predictable. Primary stress falls on the first or second syllable and in words of more than three syllables the secondary stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable. The final syllable is never stressed. In words of two syllables primary stress falls on the first syllable. [...] In words of three syllables primary stress falls either on the initial syllable [...] or on the second syllable [...] In words of four syllables primary stress falls on the first syllable with secondary stress on the penultimate syllable. [...] In words of five syllables the primary stress falls on the second syllable.
sources.locator: sect. 2.6 'Word stress', pp. 27-28 (PDF pp. 35-36 of the ANU Open Research scan, hdl:1885/145431)
sources.note: First-hand grammar of the NgK dialect. Sect. 2.6 gives a primary placement partly different from the initial-stress coding (Reid 1990): first or second syllable; second in three of six trisyllables (a.'ba.larr, de.'tye.ngi, bi.'li.rri) and in five-syllable words (a.'nim.pirr.'mi.re, a.'tye.rri.'wu.sye); initial in 2- and 4-syllable words; final never stressed. The a- words carry a class marker that Reid (p. 93) treats as a proclitic outside the phonological word, but Reid stresses detyengi initially (p. 90) and the a- of a-tyeri-wusye as a prefix (p. 94); dialect stress rules differ (p. 1).
